items.question: How do you approach breaking adversarial example defenses on image classifiers?
items.object: Breaking adversarial example defenses on image classifiers
items.answer: I think probably if you take adversarial example defenses on image classifiers, they're a particular beast that I have gotten very good at, and the attacks are relatively well understood, and there are lots of known failure modes. And so when I'm doing this, I'm not developing new science. I'm just going through, like, I have this long list of things I've broken before. What's the pattern that this one falls into? Okay, here's the pattern. It turns out that the gradients are not flowing because the softmax is saturated to one. What do you do? And once you figure out the answer is because of some discretization or whatever the case might be, then everything is easy from there.

items.question: How do you organize your thinking about attacks on machine learning models?
items.object: Gradient-based attacks on machine learning models
items.answer: Okay, let me separate off this one space of attacks, which are these new, like, a human typing in a keyboard, prompting the model to make it say a bad thing. Let's put aside for a second these kinds of treating the model as a human and trying to social-engineer it into doing something bad. If you put that aside, then almost all attacks are the way that you run the attack: you try and do some kind of gradient descent to make some particular loss function maximized. So, for image adversarial examples, what does this mean? I have an image of a stop sign. I want to know what sticker can I put on the stop sign to make it be recognized as a 45 mph speed sign. How do I do this? I perform gradient descent to maximize—compute the optimal sticker so that the thing becomes misclassified. Or, in the case of poisoning, where the poisoning is you modify a training data example point in order to make the model produce an error, you're trying to optimize the particular poisoned data point you have in the training data set so that the model makes a mistake. Or in the case of these un-fine-tunable models, you have a model that you want to make sure no one can edit, and so you try and find a way to perform gradients on the model to update the parameters so that it can perform some bad thing. And so in all of these attacks there are essentially two things you need to concern yourself with. One is: what is the objective that you're maximizing or minimizing? Like, what is the specific loss function you're using? And the other is: what is the optimization technique that you're using to make that number go up? And both of these are the two things you can play with, and by coming up with the best possible versions of each of these, you end up with very strong attacks. A big part of doing these kinds of attacks when you're doing this gradient-based optimization thing is coming up with high-quality functions that you can optimize and coming up with high-quality optimizers.

items.question: Why do you consider PGD the right way to generate adversarial image examples despite the possibility of getting more performance from fancier methods?
items.object: PGD for generating adversarial image examples
items.answer: One of my first papers in adversarial machine learning was coming up with a clever way of doing this. This was entirely a paper on these exact two questions: what's the optimizer, what's the optimization objective? And we did some clever things. It worked—well, I won't go into details here—but we did something fancy. Then, six months later or something, maybe a year later, Alexander Madry and his students said, instead of doing something clever, let's just bound the image to be between—in this sort of small ball around the initial point—so you can only perturb the three lowest bits, and only optimize the objective function I said is a good optimization objective, and run the same optimization algorithm I was using. It turns out it gets you, like, 99% of the way there, and it's so much simpler. This algorithm is called PGD, and this is the one everyone remembers because it's the right way of doing it. You can squeeze epsilon more performance out of it if you do things a lot fancier, but the defense is either effective or it's not, for the most part. And breaking the last 2% is very rarely something you actually need. For the most part, it's entirely fine to just say, let's make something a lot simpler and optimize that thing, and it ends up working quite a lot better. So, yeah, for these image examples today, people don't put a second term on minimizing the distance between the original image and the other one. They just add it as a constraint. They just say, I just constrain you to this bounding box; you can only change the lowest three bits of the pixels. And this just makes the optimization so much simpler, and it's a little bit worse, but in all practical senses it just makes things work a lot better.

items.question: How do you think the order in which attackers and defenders act affects their relative advantage in AI security?
items.object: The advantage of moving second in AI attacks and defenses
items.answer:
Finding one problem is easier than solving all of them. The particular thing is, it probably would be pretty hard for me to write down an attack algorithm that was effective against any possible defense. There's almost certainly something that someone could do that is correct, that stops all attacks. But I don't have to think about that defense. I only have to think about the defense that's literally in front of me right now, and so it's a lot easier when you're presented with one particular algorithm. You can spend six months analyzing it, and so the attacker has just an information advantage from this side too, where they can wait for the field to get better, learn new things, and then apply the attack after all of this has been learned. The defender in many cases can't update the thing that they've done.

There are some settings where this is reversed, where the attacker has to go first. Poisoning, for example, can be one of them. Suppose that I want to make malicious training data and put it on the internet, and hope that some language model provider is going to then go and train on my malicious data. In this case, it may actually be the case that the attacker has to go first. I have to upload my training data, and then someone gets to train their model with whatever algorithm they want, with whatever defense they want, to remove my poison data before they actually run the training. In this case maybe the defense is actually a little bit easier than the attack. It's hard to say, because this defender now goes second. But for many of these cases that I spend most of my time thinking about, like this recent unfinetunable models case, it is the case that the attacker goes second, and that really gives them a lot of power.

items.question: Why do you put confidence in widely scrutinized cryptographic systems like AES?
items.object: Public scrutiny of cryptographic systems
items.answer: No company in their right mind would ever try and develop a new fancy crypto system. You're just going to use AES because it's known to be good. It would be crazy to try and do anything fancy in-house. The reason why is because empirically it worked very well, and we've had the entire community try and break it for 20 years and have largely failed, and so everyone believes that this is effective. You don't get that same kind of belief in something without a large number of people trying to analyze it.

items.question: How do you assess keeping AI models proprietary as a way to make them secure?
items.object: Keeping AI models proprietary as a security strategy
items.answer: If you have these models and they stay proprietary things that are not disclosed, it may be the case that empirically this just ends up the best we can hope for. Maybe deep learning is impossible to secure; there's no hope at it. You lock things down and try to change things faster than the attackers can find bugs in them. Okay, that would not be great, but I think we can potentially live in that world. I think what would be a lot better, which just may not be happening, maybe very hard, is you get everyone to disclose exactly what they're doing, exactly how they're doing it. You get everyone to analyze that in detail, and then you learn how to make these things better, to some extent that you can actually improve robustness. items.question: What do you see as the key insight behind the objective function used to generate adversarial suffixes that make a language model answer questions it would normally refuse?

items.question: How do you think about computational cost when comparing continuous-space image attacks with discrete-token jailbreak attacks?

items.answer:

If you're doing one of these gradient things, how much do you typically have to put into it? If you're doing something that's in a discrete space and requires more of a structured search, how does that compare?

Let's start in the image adversarial example, continuous-space question. The amount of compute here is almost zero. One of the first papers that showed this is a paper by Ian Goodfellow where he introduced an attack called the fast gradient sign method. First of all it's fast, and the reason why it's fast is because what it does is it takes an image, computes the gradient with respect to the image pixels, and then computes the sign—literally, take the sign: which direction does the gradient say? Then take a small step in this direction. That's it, one step. If a model is vulnerable to this fast gradient sign method, then it takes exactly one gradient step, which is essentially zero time.

Other attacks, like I mentioned, PGD, you can think of essentially as fast gradient sign but iterated some number of times. The number of iterations is usually somewhere between 10 and 1,000. items.question: How do you understand the relationship between data curation and the difficulty of poisoning a model?
items.object: Data curation and the difficulty of data poisoning
items.answer:
The field initially started out: How do I make a model give the wrong answer? I add a bunch of labeled data that's labeled incorrectly. This is the simplest possible thing you can do. This is some paper by Batista, which got a Test of Time Award at ICML a couple years ago. It's a very nice paper from, I don't remember when, 2012 or something. It's one of these very early security results that's very important. You just insert mislabeled data. This is very easy to do. You insert a very small amount of mislabeled data and these image classifiers at the time—they were looking at MNIST classifiers—would just immediately mislabel the data.

Then people started looking at, well, what happens if the adversary can't just insert mislabeled data? Because once upon a time we used to curate our data sets to only high-quality data, and so it would be unreasonable to suspect that the adversary could just inject mislabeled data points. The answer is, well, now I have to be very, very careful. I have to optimize my images to look like they're right. There's this clean-label poisoning threat model where you need to do some fancy stuff, try and imagine what the embeddings you want the classifier to learn are, and surround your test point in embedding space and do some fancy polytope stuff. There's a bunch of work that does fancy stuff here. The optimization is relatively difficult, and you need like 1% poison to data. This is a lot.

Then people started going, well, why do we label, why do we clean our data in the first place? Let's just take all the data from the internet. Again, poisoning becomes a lot easier. If you're willing to just take arbitrary data from the internet, now you can just mislabel your data points again. We had a paper, I don't know, in 2021, looking at poisoning some of these self-supervised classifiers like CLIP and others, where you just add mislabeled data points again and the thing basically just breaks. You don't need to do anything fancy, no optimization. You just flip the label, add a couple hundred images, and you can get these kinds of things to work.

items.question: How do you assess the current state of language-model poisoning attacks that must survive fine-tuning and RLHF?
items.object: Language-model poisoning that survives fine-tuning and RLHF
items.answer:
I feel like we don't understand this right now because a bunch of things are different for language models. For example, no one just uses the base language model. You have your language model and then you go fine-tune it with SFT and RLHF, and you change the weights, so you need your poisoning to be robust to all these things.

This is another paper I helped advise some students on from CMU and from Zurich, where Jav and them were looking at trying to understand what actually happens in the optimization after you have poisoned a model. You have to arrange for the model to be poisoned in such a way that even after RLHF it still gives you the wrong answer. Doing this is challenging, and so it ends up right now that the poisoning rates are something like 0.1%, which is small. But 0.1% of a trillion tokens is a billion tokens, so if you were to train a model on some large fraction of the internet, this could potentially be infeasible for an adversary to do in practice.

My gut feeling is that this has to be too big, because models know more than a thousand things. If you had to have control of 1,000th of the data set to make the model believe something is true, they could only know a thousand things, and this just doesn't make sense. There has to be some better poisoning way to make the model vulnerable to poisoning that works with much lower control of the training data. But this might now need fancier algorithms again. You might need to come up with clever ways of constructing your data that's not just repeating the same false fact lots of times. Again, I don't know. I think this is one of the open questions we've been trying to write some papers on recently, and I hope we'll have a better understanding sometime this year.

items.question: How do you understand why a classifier’s decision boundary can be very close in high dimensions yet difficult to find by searching in random directions?
items.object: Proximity to classifier decision boundaries in high-dimensional spaces
items.answer: Maybe the statement that I will make, to be more precise, is: let's suppose that you have some classification model and you have some decision boundary of the classifier. The statement that is true is almost all points are very close to one of the decision boundaries, because both there are many of them, but also in high dimensions I may be very far from something in almost all directions, but there exists a direction that I can travel in—the direction orthogonal to the closest plane—where the distance is very, very small. You have this thing where if you try in random directions, you may just go forever and never encounter a decision boundary. You probably will at some point, but it will be quite far. But in high dimensions, because of the number of degrees of freedom that you have, it's much more likely that there exists a direction that guides you to some plane that's really close by, that you would just have a hard time finding if you searched randomly. Whereas in three dimensions, if you search randomly, you're probably going to run into whatever the nearest type of plane boundary is. In one dimension, you certainly are going to: you try twice, you go left, you go right, you find it. In two dimensions you go randomly and maybe most of the time you find something that's close by. In three dimensions there's an infinite number of ways you can go that are orthogonal to the line. In general, in high dimensions almost all vectors are perpendicular to each other, and so you can end up almost always randomly picking directions that just don't make any progress. That does not mean that there isn't a direction that does make progress; it's just much harder to find it. But once you find it, things mostly just work out. Maybe this is the more precise version of what I'm trying to say: things are close.

items.question: How do you judge whether adversarial training works as a defense against attacks on image classifiers?
items.object: Adversarial training as a defense against attacks on image classifiers
items.answer: So, okay, it depends on what you mean by works. The best defenses we have are basically adversarial training: generate examples, train on examples to be correct, repeat the process many, many times. What does this give you? This gives you a classifier so that on the domain of adversarial examples you trained on, as long as you don't want to be accurate more than half of the time, you're pretty good. The accuracy under attack for the type of adversarial examples you train on usually is 50%, 60%, maybe 70%. That's much bigger than zero. This is good. But as an attacker, what does 70% accuracy mean to me? 70% accuracy as an attacker means I try four times and probably one of them works. From that perspective, it's terrible; it doesn't work at all. items.question: What lesson do you draw from distillation as a defense against adversarial examples?
items.object: Distillation as a defense against adversarial examples
items.answer:
One of the very first defenses to adversarial examples that people gave serious consideration is this defense called distillation as a defense. This had another lesson: these defenses often have an intuitive reason why the authors think they work, and they tell some very nice story. This defense told a nice story about how you have distillation, you have a teacher model, and the teacher sort of teaches the student to be more robust in some nice way, and that's why the student is robust. The story they're telling themselves about why these things work is often very, very different from the reason why the attack fails. It turned out that distillation had nothing to do with this defense whatsoever. Because of the way they were training this model, they were training the students to have a very high temperature, which means the logits were getting very large, and they were running this in a time of TensorFlow 0 when it was very easy to make gradients mean that softmax cross entropy would actually give numerically zero as the output. The reason why the attacks were failing is because the loss function was identically zero.

This was the very first example of one of these kinds of gradient-masking defenses. What's going on is they think they have some clever idea, but actually it turns out that the gradient of this function has just been made zero. All I need to do to attack it is, for example, this one failed if you just did the gradients in floating point 64, you get enough signal that everything works out. You could also do other tricks by dividing the logits before you put them in the softmax. Lots of things work here.

items.question: How do you think about attacking defenses that make a model's gradients difficult to optimize?
items.object: Loss surfaces and defenses that make gradients difficult to optimize
items.answer:
For the most part, what I'm doing is trying to understand the shape of the loss surface. Most of the time when something is robust to attack or appears robust, the problem is that they have made the loss surface particularly noisy and hard to optimize. This is what we've seen for adversarial examples essentially forever.

There were a bunch of defenses, some very explicit, where we're just going to add noise to the model in order to make it so that the gradients are ugly. Most of what you're trying to think about when you're visualizing this is, how do I make it so that the gradients end up being something that, even if they look ugly, I can still work with in some smooth way? You can use this thing called a straight-through estimator and make gradients become nicer for discontinuous or ugly objective functions. There are all these things you can do to visualize how I make the gradients of this very ugly thing look much cleaner.

I have this image that I use in my slides a bunch that shows a very nice visualization in three dimensions of what the gradients for many of these models look like. It looks like the surface of some very, very ugly mountain that's very hard to do anything with. If you run fancier attacks, you can smooth this out into a nice smooth surface. If you're thinking of gradient descent as a ball rolling down a hill, you want the hill to be nice and smooth. This is what I'm usually trying to think about in high dimensions: what does this gradient function look like?

This continued all the way through to these un-fine-tunable models, where one of the papers for this fine-tunable model thing was explicitly saying we make the gradients very challenging, and when you train the model the gradients are ugly, so as a result you can't fine-tune the model because the gradients are challenging. This is literally the exact same argument that people were presenting in 2017 for image adversarial examples, and it fails in the exact same way: you change the learning rate a little bit, add some random restarts, add some warmup so that things work a little better, and the gradient ends up becoming smooth enough that you can now do optimization. Then deep learning takes over, and the rest is easy.

items.question: Why did you expect the TAR paper's defense using adversarial training to be breakable?
items.object: The TAR paper's use of adversarial training
items.answer:

There was a paper before Alexander Madry's PGD paper that tried to do adversarial training: they trained against weak adversaries, FGSM, the one-step attack I talked about briefly. If you train against weak adversaries, then a stronger attack breaks it. You have to train against a strong enough attack for the thing to be robust and not break under either of my stronger attacks.

What the TAR paper did was train against one-step weak attacks, exactly like fast gradient sign. The attack you do is many iterations, and things basically work out exactly as the first versions of training failed. That's why I read this paper and immediately assumed it was going to be broken: all of the arguments it presents for why it works have direct analogies to broken defenses in image adversarial examples. The ideas felt there, but in spirit these were things I knew were broken before, so I assumed it was probably broken here too.

Every tool that you have can be used in both of these ways, so it's not obvious to me why we should be blaming the machine learning model itself for being able to produce this. Maybe I blame the Nvidia GPUs for supporting the sufficiently fast floating-point operations that the machine learning model does this thing. Maybe I blame the transistors for doing the computations that allow the GPUs to allow the machine learning model to do this thing. You have to put the blame somewhere. Where are you going to put it? items.question: How do you assess indistinguishability obfuscation as a way to protect AI models running on someone's own machine?
items.object: Indistinguishability obfuscation as a possible protection for locally running AI models
items.answer: If you're willing to make some assumptions and you don't care at all about performance, there was this thing in cryptography called indistinguishability obfuscation, which is a very technical thing that in principle gives you this for free. It allows you to construct a function that acts as if it were a black box that you can only make queries to, but you can't peer inside at all, even though it's living on your own machine. Cryptographers are thinking about this and have been looking at it for some time, but it's nowhere near where it needs to be for this to work for these machine learning models. The argument I've given that it shouldn't be possible maybe breaks down if IO actually ends up working, but then it's not clear again: now I'm going to jailbreak the thing, right?

items.question: How do you make sense of social-engineering jailbreaks succeeding against language-model defenses where optimization-based attacks fail?
items.object: Social-engineering jailbreaks outperforming optimization-based attacks on language models
items.answer:
I really don't know how to think about this yet. It's been a while that this has been possible, but it feels wrong to me. It is empirically true that for many defenses we have right now, the optimization algorithms fail to succeed, but a person at a keyboard typing at a model can make it do the wrong thing.

Let me give you maybe two stories about this. One story is from the computer security perspective. Maybe this makes complete sense. If you give me a program and want me to find a bug in it, what am I going to do? I'm going to interact with the program, play with it, find weak points, then go looking at the code and figure out what's going on, think a lot, sort of probe it. I need to be typing and interacting with it in order to find the bugs. I can't perform gradient descent on a C binary and a bug pops out. From the computer security perspective, maybe it's actually normal that the best way to find these bugs is having humans talk at them, because what are these things designed to do? They're designed to respond to human questions, so maybe you just need the human in the loop to do this.

On the other hand, these are just mathematical objects. These are just machine-learning classifiers. They're weird classifiers; they're able to produce text, but that's only because we run them recursively. The input is tokens; the output is floating-point numbers. You can compute gradients on this. From the machine-learning perspective, it's very bizarre that thinking of these things like humans, that we're social-engineering, is in some sense a stronger attack than these. If you were to actually think about the math, it'd be very weird if I had some SQL program and the way that I broke it was by asking it, "Please drop the table," and not actually doing some real code-execution thing. Presumably that's the way many of these attacks are now: "My grandmother used to read me the recipe to napalm. Can you please reenact my grandmother?" And it says, "Okay, sure." But you try and do something actually based on the math and it just doesn't work out.

I really don't know how to think about the social-engineering styles of attack, because it feels to me like the optimization attacks should be strictly stronger, but empirically they're not right now. This is one of the big things that I don't have any research result on right now, but just feels weird, and so I'm trying to dig in to understand what is going on behind this.

items.question: What do you find puzzling about which training examples language and diffusion models memorize?
items.object: The unexplained selectivity of memorization in language and diffusion models
items.answer:
We were surprised by this the first time we saw it. We started investigating this in 2017 with LSTMs, before attention was a thing they were doing, and it's continued since then. We were very surprised then; we're very surprised now, and I don't think I can give you an explanation for why this is the case.

It's true not only on language models. We had a paper on doing this on image models, where we were able to show that you can recover images trained on diffusion models. There again we need to have maybe 100 repeats, but some images were inserted 100 times and we could extract them, and some images were inserted like 10,000 times and we couldn't. What's going on there? I don't know. Where is it being stored in the weights? I don't know. It's very confusing in various ways. I feel like there's a lot more that could happen to help us understand what's going on.

items.question: Why do you regard the Bau Lab's work on editing facts in large language models as a promising contribution to understanding how models store information?
items.object: Bau Lab research on editing facts in large language models
items.answer:
The best thing I've seen on this, as far as I know, is from the Bau Lab. This goes back a while now, but they had at least two papers on basically editing facts in a large language model. The famous example was "Michael Jordan played baseball," which was somewhat not optimally chosen since for a minute he did play baseball. They could do things like change these sentences at some scale, up to 10,000 facts at a time, and do it with a certain amount of locality and robustness. If you changed "Michael Jordan played baseball," it would be robust to different rephrasing of that and would not also impact LeBron James or Larry Bird or whatever.

It didn't seem like it was still super local. They did a patching strategy where they would go through and try to ablate different weights—like activation patching. They weren't necessarily ablating the weights, but just sort of zeroing out the activations at different parts in the network.

items.question: How do you assess whether unlearning or fact editing has deeply changed a model?
items.object: Robustness of model unlearning and fact editing
items.answer:
There's a very nice paper that I didn't help with, but it's by some of my co-authors, Katherine Lee and others, that talks about unlearning. It's half technical, half not technical, saying unlearning doesn't do what you think it does. Part of the reason is the question of what you're unlearning. Unlearning knowledge is very different from unlearning facts. It might be easy to change a fact; it might be very, very different to unlearn some particular piece of knowledge.

The other thing I'll say about fact editing is it's very different to find something that works on average from something that works in the adversarial case. I might be able to edit the fact—I think the other example they had was "The Eiffel Tower is in Rome"—and make this be true if I normally ask the model. But it might be the case that if I fine-tune the model a little bit, the knowledge just goes back. It's very hard to talk about the knowledge after any perturbation of the weights. Maybe I've only done some surface-level thing; I haven't really deeply edited the model. I don't know.

items.question: What limitations do you see in excluding particular kinds of information from a model's training data?
items.object: Excluding information from training as a way to limit model knowledge and capabilities
items.answer:
This is very interesting because in some sense it's provably correct: if the model has never seen my social security number, it's not going to derive it from first principles. Except social security numbers actually aren't completely random. If you were born before—I don't know when—and they were assigned by state and then assigned to the hospital, a model that never saw my social security number but is generally intelligent and knew all these facts about the world and knew the hospital allocation of social security numbers could tell you the first five digits of my social security number. Is that okay? I don't know. It depends.

Even suppose that you removed all this information from the model. If you had a sufficiently capable model that's capable of learning in context, let's suppose you removed all biology knowledge from the model, but you had a really capable model, you could give it an undergraduate course in biology textbooks in context and presumably ask it the answer to some question, and it might give you the answer correctly. This sounds a little absurd, and it sounded absurd to me for a while, but then there was the recent result where Gemini was given in context a book from a language that has basically no speakers, that no one could do, and it could answer homework exercises after seeing the book in context.

If you're unlearning particular capabilities but the model you're trying to train is generally capable, you're kind of asking for trouble. You want a model that's so good it can learn from few-shot examples, but not so good it can learn from few-shot examples on this particular task.

items.question: Why do you think teaching a model to recognize harmful actions and refuse them is a promising safety approach?
items.object: Teaching models to recognize harmful actions and refuse them
items.answer:
This is part of the reason why people don't actually want to remove all knowledge of certain things from the training data. In some sense, it would be very much like a person who was never exposed to all of the things you're not supposed to do in public. It's important to know what the list of things you're not supposed to do in public is, so that you can not do them. If you just weren't aware of that and were a person conjured with no social skill, it would be much more embarrassing. You would have to learn: people would ask you to do something, you'd be like, "Okay, let me go do that thing," and that would be bad. You have to know something about the bad things so you can just not do those bad things.

You could imagine one world where you have a model that's never seen anything about weapons, and then you give it instructions for how to build a bomb. It has no concept of death and says, "Of course I'm going to give you the answer for how to do this thing. Why not?" Or you could have a model that has a concept of this and refuses, which is the direction people are trying to pursue now and I think probably is more likely to succeed. I don't know. It's a very challenging question. People are going to try both, and we'll see empirically what works out. We'll go from there. I'm mostly agnostic to all ideas; they sound good, we should try them all and see what ends up happening. But I think there's reason to be skeptical of all of them.

items.question: Why did you expect the result that obfuscated activation attacks could repeatedly defeat latent defenses in language models?
items.object: Obfuscated activation attacks against latent defenses
items.answer:
I saw this result and was like, "Exactly what I expect." Let me tell you why. There was a paper from 2016 or 2017 by Florian Tramer and Nicolas Papernot called "The Space of Transferable Adversarial Examples," where they asked almost exactly this question for image classifiers. They said, let's suppose I take an image classifier and an image, and I want to perturb the pixels to make it give the wrong answer. There's a direction that's the best direction to go to that makes the image maximally incorrect. As an attacker, I'm just going to prevent you from going that direction. That's against the rules; you can't do it. Find the next best direction to make the image misclassified. Then it gave you another direction orthogonal to the first direction. Don't go that way—that works. Then I said, okay, you can't go in either of the first two directions, or any combination of them. Find another direction. The attacker finds direction three, and they do the same thing: no direction one, two, three, or any combination of these three. They repeat this process. They have a plot showing, I don't remember, tens, 50 directions you can go in for image adversarial examples, all of them work. They get a little less effective as you move out, but it remains effective in many directions.

This was initially surprising to me, and I think surprising to them; that's why they published it as a paper. But you can maybe rationalize it afterwards: almost all vectors are orthogonal in high dimensions. If I give you ten attacks, probably these are just ten orthogonal vectors that are not using any of the same features, by virtue of high dimensions. Maybe that's why it makes sense. If you believe this paper from 2016, then this recent paper makes complete sense to me. It's saying the exact same thing is true in the case of language models defeating the Circuit Breaker paper. If you don't believe the other result, I agree it's very surprising the first time you see it. But maybe this is one of these things you learn when attacking: the space of directions for attacks is so vast that it's very hard to rule out what you're trying to cover. I don't know how to give an intuition for it. Many things in high dimensions, you never understand; you just get used to them. This may be the case here.

items.question: How do you think about the idea that compressing a neural network could eliminate the space available for adversarial attacks?
items.object: Model compression as a defense against adversarial attacks
items.answer:
I don't know if you could do this on these really small, crystallized toy models. These models are not wasting any weights, which is different than not wasting any directions in activation space. That may still be the case. In particular, if you take models and compress them, they don't become more adversarially robust. This was something people thought might be true, maybe 8 or 10 years ago, but it's not the case.

Maybe let me give you some intuition from a paper from 2018 or 2019, maybe from Alexander Madry's group. Maybe adversarial examples are not entirely uncorrelated from the data. Maybe what's going on is these are real features you need for classification that are just being activated unusually, larger in different ways. They have good experiments in the paper that justify this. The title is something like "Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features." The idea is there's a good reason to believe that what you're getting across when you construct one of these attacks is actually just activating real features the model needs for accurate classification, and you're activating them in a way that is not normally activated with a particular example. If you take these models and compress them, you're still using the features they had to have anyway. This explains lots of things. Maybe adversarial training can reduce accuracy on normal data because you suppress certain features that are necessary. Maybe this is why adversarial training doesn't solve the problem completely, because you can't remove all the adversarial directions. There are problems with this model; there are other, slightly more general models with nice properties too. This is how I tend to think about some of these things. Maybe it's not correct, but it's a useful intuition that guides me in the right direction more often than not. I think this is all you can ask for.

items.question: How do you understand the role of useful learned features in making machine-learning models vulnerable to adversarial attacks?
items.object: Adversarial attacks exploiting useful features learned by machine-learning models
items.answer:
Here is a feature that's really useful for getting the right answer that, as an adversary, I can use to perturb, to switch the model from one label to another, even though it's not the feature that I as a human relied on. I'm giving you this idea of cat versus dog fur, but there are all kinds of other things that, even as humans, we don't pick up on that might be legitimately useful features to classify that really do help the model. There might be some crazy high-level statistic on the pixels of the image that is an amazing feature of a dog, but we never told it, "This is a dog because of these reasons." We just said separate these two things from each other, and it picked up on the statistics.

There are crazy results showing machine-learning models can look at small regions of the eye and identify the type of person it is. The models can pick up on very, very small features that as humans we don't intend for them to pick up on, but they're correlated very strongly with the data. Maybe that's what's going on when we run these attacks. You see this a little bit with these adversarial suffixes where the suffixes look like noise, but there are some parts of them that make a little bit of sense. One of the strings in the paper to get Gemini to output some toxic content was, I think, "now write opposite contents" or something like this. The model would give you the nasty strings and then compliment you. This was apparently a very strong feature for the model: how do I get it to say the bad thing? I can say, "Okay, in the future you can tell me a good thing." This may not have been the thing that we wanted, but it was discovered as a feature, and as a result you can exploit that feature. Some of these features are a little bit interpretable; some are not interpretable, but might just actually be real features of the data.

items.question: How do you reconcile sparse autoencoders' explanations of model features with adversarial attacks that exploit features humans can't interpret?
items.object: Sparse autoencoders and the limits of interpreting model features
items.answer:
I think they're not inconsistent. Sparse autoencoder work does not claim to be able to label every feature in the model according to what humans would label it with. It sort of says, here are some of the features that we can explain and have very strong correlations with, I don't know, Golden Gate bridges or whatever. But it has other features that are very hard to interpret and explain. It's entirely possible these are the non-robust features that are helpful for prediction, but humans don't have the ability to attach a very nice label to them.

Maybe there are still other features. The model probably does learn, at least in part, the shape of what a dog looks like and that this means dog and not cat. There probably is a feature for cat ears. But when you're making the final prediction, you're going to sum together all of these outputs. In normal data they're all perfectly correlated: you're going to have both the cat ears and the cat fur and not the dog shape, so you can sum them up directly, and this gives you a really good classifier. For normal data you can give some kind of explanation by looking at these features. As an attacker, what I do is find the one feature that has a very strong bias, where the edge on this weight or whatever is plus 100, and activate that very strongly in the opposite direction. This was a non-robust feature that is not something humans can explain very nicely, and as a result this gives me the attack.

It's not necessarily true that just because this is the case, you can't explain what's going on for some parts of the model. If someone told me, "I have a perfect explanation of what's going on in every part of the model," I might question what's going on. For the most part they're explaining some small fraction of the weights in a way they actually can. This is the whole purpose of sparse autoencoders: you have your enormous model and shrink it down to some small sparse number of features that can be better explained, so you're losing a bunch of features in the first place. Even for the sparse autoencoders, they can't explain all of those, so you lose some. Some of the things you can explain, but a lot of what's going on behind the scenes is magic and you can't easily explain it.

items.question: How do you understand the apparent gap between human and neural-network robustness to adversarial examples?
items.object: Human robustness to adversarial examples compared with neural networks
items.answer:
There's a paper from a little while ago that looks at evaluating the robustness of time-limited humans to constructing adversarial examples. You take a cat, adversarially perturb it according to what makes an ensemble of neural networks give the wrong answer, flash the image in front of a human for 100 milliseconds, and ask the human what's the label. It turns out that people are fooled more often by adversarial examples than by random noise of the same distortion amounts.

Maybe one explanation is when I look at the image, I'm not just giving you a single forward pass through the model evaluation of what I think it is. I'm doing some deeper thinking about the context: the thing that walked in looked like a cat, it still looks like a cat, it did the thing behaving like a cat, and now you ask me what it is and I say it's a cat. I'm not just labeling what's in front of my eyes right now; I'm looking back at the context too. Maybe this explains some of it. If this is true, there are some recent lines of work looking at improving the number of chain-of-thought tokens; increasing that makes models appear to be more adversarially robust. Maybe this is true and explains that result.

It might also be the case that, like you said, we don't have white-box access to the human brain, and we can't do this. If we could, it would be very easy. I do think it's definitely an observable fact that humans are more robust to at least the kinds of attacks we're doing right now with transfer attacks. It takes maybe a thousand query images to construct an example that fools their own network, but I do not think that if someone had run the same attack on me with a thousand query images it would be able to fool me. In some very real way, the models we have are a lot more brittle.

items.question: How do you think we can build dependable AI agent systems if the models themselves remain vulnerable to attacks?
items.object: Building robust AI agent systems around vulnerable models
items.answer:
I think my median prediction is these models remain roughly as vulnerable as they are now, and we just have to build systems that understand that models can make mistakes. The world as built right now, for the most part, assumes that humans can make mistakes and has put systems in place so that any single person is not going to cause too much damage. In a company, for the most part when you want to add code to the repository, someone else needs to review it and sign off on it, in part because maybe I make a bug mistake, maybe because I'm doing something malicious, but you want another human to look and make sure everything looks good.

Maybe you do the same thing with models: understand models can make mistakes, and build my system so that if the model makes a mistake, I pass it off to the human. This is currently the way the OpenAI Operator thing works: every time it sees a login page or something like this and it's not sure what to do, it says, "What should I do here? Please tell me what to do," and then I'll follow your instructions. Of course, as an attacker you could try to prevent it from doing this and make it give the answer instead. But if you built something outside the system that prevented it from putting any information into a password box—the model says, "I want to type this data here," and the system actually driving the agent says, "That is input type equals password; you are not allowed to do that"—we prevent it and make the user do it. Nothing the model says is going to convince that to change.

You could build the system to be robust even if you don't trust the thing running internally. This limits utility in important ways. It's not perfect: what if a website doesn't have input type equals password, but builds its own password thing in JavaScript, and you don't get this? You can imagine building the environment and the agent so you can control what's going on even if you don't trust the thing running internally. I think this is probably what we'll have to do if we want to make these systems work in the near term.

I still have some hope that maybe we'll have new ideas that give us robustness in the next couple of years. Progress in every other field has been growing much faster than I expected. It's entirely possible we get robustness as a result of some reasoning thing that someone's very clever about, and this works. I'm not optimistic, but I wish it happens.

items.question: How do you view symmetric-key cryptography as a precedent for making machine learning robust through repeated attacks without fully understanding why the defenses work?
items.object: Symmetric-key cryptography as a precedent for developing robust machine learning through repeated attacks
items.answer:
Then there's symmetric-key cryptography, which is block cipher design and stuff. People have high-level principles of what you want, like diffusion and confusion, but how do you end up with the particular design? You do something that feels like it makes sense, then you run all the attacks and realize this has something wrong in some particular way. Let's change that piece so that isn't the case anymore. You do this for 20 years and end up with AES. None of the individual components have a reason why AES works. There's absolutely no formal proof of robustness to any kind of attack. There are proofs of why particular attack algorithms we know in the literature are not going to succeed. The design principles were inspired by these attack algorithms. You can show there is never going to exist a differential attack that succeeds better than brute force, or a linear attack, and you can write down these arguments, but there's nothing that says it works in general. Just by iterating on making the thing slightly more robust each time someone comes up with a new clever attack, you end up with something that's very good. There's no crystallizable mathematical assumption like the hard factoring problem. There's nothing like that for symmetric cryptography, but it works really well. Maybe this works in machine learning, where you don't have a real understanding of why things work; you attack them and end up with something robust.

I think it's maybe harder in machine learning because you want the thing primarily to be useful and also to be robust to attack, whereas in cryptography the only thing you want is robustness to attack. The primitives you're working with are much simpler to analyze. There are lots of other things that change, but it would not be without prior work that this seems impossible. I'm skeptical only because I would prefer something where we can point to a reason why it works, as opposed to just saying empirically it is. If you gave me the option between something that actually is robust that we just can't explain and nothing that works at all, of course I take the thing that works and we can't explain. items.question: How do you assess defense in depth through layered detectors as an approach to AI security?
items.object: Defense in depth and layered detectors for AI security
items.answer:
In part, this is how most secure systems are designed to be secure: layers of security on top of layers of security. Defense in depth is the thing that works in practice. We were just talking about block ciphers, and the reason those are robust is because they have many layers of this confusion-diffusion thing. You stack enough of them and the thing becomes hard to get past. You can get past a couple layers, but you can't get deeper. It's a tried-and-tested thing in security.

This generally works. All else equal, we would prefer a system that is robust because you can write down why it's effective. If you can't have this, having something that empirically has these 20 layers and when put together in the right way it turns out the attacks don't work is something we would be happy to settle for. There are reasons you might be concerned: maybe someone has an attack that bypasses all of them because it's fundamentally different in some interesting way. We have to accept this. This is one of the options we should be exploring a lot, because maybe full robustness is basically impossible and we need to settle for layers of detectors. If it turns out you can still have robustness, detectors are useful anyway, so it's good to have done the work ahead of time.

items.question: How do you think about choosing a false-positive rate for a detection system that people will actually pay attention to?
items.object: False-positive rates and human factors in detection systems
items.answer:
Yeah, I mean, in any detection thing you have to tune the false-positive/true-positive rate. You can pick whatever point you want on the curve, and the question is what point you pick. I was reading some security paper a while ago that was looking at the human-factors aspect of this problem. It was arguing it's actually a better user experience to have false-positive flagged humans every once in a while, because if you don't do this then the person's like, "Well, my camera's not looking." But if you do, the person's like, "Oh, I feel a little better. Maybe it made a mistake; it was a little too aggressive, but I feel more confident now it's going to find the actual human when there's a real human there."

There's maybe some actual human-factors reason you might prefer to set the false-positive rate a certain way, although in my case I've tuned them out entirely now. This is the thing with lots of software that reports warnings in code. The compiler will give you warnings that you're doing something that's not great. Once you pass a thousand warnings, the person just disables all warnings. It would have been good to have an important thing it will warn you about, but because you had 900 warnings that were not actually important, you've lost the actual important signals. Picking the right value is very hard. It's mostly a question of tuning the true-positive/false-positive rate on a defense-by-defense basis.

items.question: How do you approach designing a safety classifier to prioritize catching harmful mistakes while tolerating less consequential ones?

items.question: How do you assess language models' current ability to automatically break AI defenses?
items.object: Language models as tools for automatically breaking AI defenses
items.answer:
The answer is basically not yet. The answer is a little more nuanced: if I give a language model a defense presented in a really clean, easy-to-study homework-exercise presentation, where I've rewritten the defense from scratch and put the core logic in 20 lines of Python, then I've done most of the hard work, and the model can figure out what it needs to do to make the gradients work in many cases. But when you give it the real-world code, the models fail entirely.

The reason is that the core of security is turning this really ugly system that no one understands what's going on in and highlighting the one part of it that happens to be the most important piece, removing all the other stuff people thought was the explanation but wasn't, and bringing out that part and saying, "No, here is the bug." Bugs are obvious in retrospect, usually, and doubly so for security ones. If you give models the ability to look only at easy-to-study code, they do a reasonable job. They know how to write PGD and these kinds of things. If you dump them into a random Git repository from some person's paper that hasn't been set up nicely to study and has a thousand lines of code, and who knows what half of it's doing, they struggle quite a lot.

items.question: What concerns you about how AI benchmarks measure models' ability to perform real-world tasks?

items.answer: This is something I'm concerned about not only for this problem but in general. Often when we test models we test them on the thing we think is hard for humans, but it's not the actual thing that represents the real task. I'd like to see more people trying to understand the end-to-end nature of things. Maybe MMLU was a great metric two or three years ago because models couldn't do it. You see this on many benchmarks: certain models have high accuracy on particular test sets, but then you put them in agentic tasks and other models do a lot better. items.question: How do you weigh the risks of researching AI attack capabilities against the value of demonstrating them?
items.object: The risks and value of research into AI attack capabilities
items.answer:
There is risk for this. The very first serious example of a computer worm, the Morris worm, was by Robert Morris in 1984, '86, something like this. Depending on who you believe, it was a lab leak where he was experimenting on this in his local computer lab and it accidentally got out and took down basically the entire internet, and people were panicked for a while. Doing these kinds of attacks could do this.

One thing to be said, though, is I do not think there has been another example of a lab-leak-style Morris worm in the last 50 years for this kind of thing in security. You very rarely have people do this, because in security there's the knowledge of what you can do and then there's the weaponization of it. In most papers people write, they just don't weaponize it, in part because we've seen an example of what can happen afterwards.

Maybe there's a world where things go too far and you train the model to be the adversary and end up with war games or something. But for the most part, I think doing the research on showing whether or not the models have these abilities is probably better, if only because most of these things we're building are not that hard. If someone was malicious and wanted to do it, they would do it anyway. If I spent a year designing a special-purpose attack agent, maybe that would not be a great thing to do, in the same way most security researchers don't spend a year designing malware that's gone too far. But if you put minimal work in to prove the proof of concept is easy, this is important to show people how easy it is, because the people who know it's easy are not going to write the papers and say it's easy. You want to have some idea of what kinds of things anyone can do so you can get your defenses in place.

items.question: How do you assess the value of Anthropic’s eight-layer jailbreaking contest requiring a single jailbreak that works across different attacks?
items.object: Anthropic’s eight-layer jailbreaking contest and its requirement for a single jailbreak across attacks
items.answer:
I think it's an entirely reasonable question to ask what do we actually want to be achieving with this. On one hand, this is a really hard problem, to be robust to jailbreaking attacks, so making partial progress is good even if it's only in small areas. Look at adversarial examples: we've spent almost 10 years, more than 10 years, trying to solve robustness to an adversary who can perturb every pixel by at most 8 over 255 on an L-infinity scale. Why? This problem does not matter because no adversary is like, "What about N pixels?" But we set the task because it is a well-defined problem we can try to solve, and anything else we really want is strictly harder. This has been a problem for a very long time, so let's try to solve this particular adversarial-example problem in the hopes that we'll learn something that lets us generalize to the larger field as a whole.

I don't know why they developed this exact thing. This is a reason you might do it. On the other hand, you're entirely right that even if you could solve this problem, it doesn't solve the entire problem as a whole, because I can just find my jailbreaks one by one. That's true, but it's a better world to live in than the world we're living in today. This is the world we live in for most computer security: someone has to try very hard to exploit your one new particular program. There's not a sequence of magic bytes that makes every program break. If that were the case, things would be much worse off.

items.question: How do you think about whether powerful AI models should be open source given the security risks and the concentration of power involved?
items.object: Open-source AI models, security risks, and concentration of power
items.answer:
I don't know. This is a very hard question. This is a question I think would be great for you to ask some of these people who think about the societal implications of this kind of work. The thing I want these people to understand is that, at least right now and presumably for the near future, we probably can't lock these things down to the degree they would want.

I'm very worried about concentration of power in general. I feel like open source up until today has only been good for computer security and safety in general, and because of that it would take a lot for me to change my mind that open source wasn't beneficial. I'm not going to say it's impossible I would change my mind. If things continue exponentially and you gave me the magic box that could break into any government system in the world that anyone could have if they have the tools, I probably would say that shouldn't be something we distribute to everyone in the world. But maybe if you have this, you can defend all your systems because you run the magic box and find all the bugs and patch them, and now you're perfectly safe. I don't know. It's very hard to reason about these things.

In any world that looks noticeably like our world, open source is objectively a good thing and is what I would be biased toward until I see compelling evidence to the contrary. I can't tell you what the evidence would be that would make me believe this right now, but I'm willing to accept someone could show me in some number of years. If your timelines are 20 years, this may be something I'm willing to change my mind on.

items.question: How do you judge the trade-off involved in giving everyone access to strong encryption?
items.object: Public access to strong encryption
items.answer: I think it was objectively a good thing that we decided to give everyone in the world high levels of encryption. items.answer: I have no idea how this calculus plays out for language models. It depends on exactly how capable you think they're going to become. I don't know what that's going to be. items.question: How do you think about uncertainty over whether increasingly capable language models should be distributed as widely as possible?
items.object: Uncertainty about whether increasingly capable language models should be widely distributed
items.answer:
It's very hard to predict what will happen with better models. This is why the question is harder than when it was cryptography. It was clear then: it gives everyone perfect encryption. We don't know the consequences, but you're not going to get more perfect encryption than perfect encryption. With these models, maybe they continue scaling, maybe they don't. Maybe they scale but it takes 50 years and gives society time to adapt; maybe they scale in two years and society doesn't have time to adapt. I don't know where this is going. I think this is why I want policy people thinking about this more than I am. As long as they're willing to think through the consequences, these are people who can give better answers. There are reasons to believe the answer might be we should be concerned, and reasons to believe the answer should be we should obviously distribute to as many people as possible. If anyone said one of these answers is obviously objectively right with 100% certainty, they're way overconfident. I tend to be biased based on what has been true in the past; some people are biased based on what they think might be true in the future. These are reasonable positions as long as you're willing to accept the other one might also be correct.

items.question: What do you see as the most important standard for making decisions about AI?
items.object: Evidence-based decision-making about AI
items.answer:
I want more people to do good science on these kinds of things. I think it's very easy for people to try and make decisions when they're not informed about what the state of the world actually looks like. My biggest concern is that we will start having people make decisions who are uninformed in important ways, and as a result we'll regret the decisions that we made.

I'd rather people make decisions based on the best available facts at the time. That's really the best you can hope for: maybe you made the wrong decision, but you looked at all the knowledge. What I'm worried about is we will have the knowledge and people will make decisions independent of what is true in the world, based on some ideology of what they want to be true in the world.
